summary.text: What is the criterion: environmental justice & vulnerable communities?

Just transitions has been defined as "ensuring that no one is left behind or pushed behind in the transition to low-carbon and environmentally sustainable economies and societies" (Committee for Development Policy, 2023, p. 1). This environmental justice & vulnerable communities criterion seeks to understand the future adaptation scenarios under consideration through a lens that safeguards against the underrepresentation or exclusion of any groups as climate adaptation planning faces transitions.

Environmental justice (EJ) is "the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people, regardless of race, culture, national origin, or income, in the development, adoption, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws, regulations, and policies" (Delta Stewardship Council, n.d.).

This criterion addresses EJ through the lens of vulnerable communities. Vulnerability is defined by Delta Adapts as "the intersection of exposure to climate hazards, sensitivity to those hazards, and adaptive capacity, or the ability to recover from and adapt to climate hazards. Delta Adapts identifies the communities with the highest social vulnerability to climate hazards, meaning the communities with high sensitivity and low adaptive capacity to flooding, extreme heat, and wildfire" (Delta Stewardship Council, 2021, p. xi).

Vulnerability classifications for Delta communities were obtained from the Delta Stewardship Council's Vulnerability to Climate Change in the Delta interactive map (Delta Stewardship Council, 2020). Categories of vulnerability included in this tool are Moderate, High, or Highest, based on weighting of 14 indicators (Delta Stewardship Council, 2020):
It is important to note that the lowest vulnerability classification across the Delta is "Moderate" - and thus all Delta communities are considered vulnerable communities in varying degrees.
82.6% of Just Transitions interviewees think decision-making processes in the Delta are not equitable and fair.
Only 8.7% said decision-making is equitable and fair.
Citing power dynamic discrepancies, monetary influences, and infringement or outright violation of water rights, interviewees made their viewpoints known:
"The whole framework of salinity management in the Delta is fundamentally flawed by the institutional issues and the dominance of financial interests."
"The decision-makers are coming from different agencies with different missions, different agendas, different levels of resources. So is it equitable? No. And is it cohesive? No."

"Overall, the groups with the most funding can hire the very expensive consultants with the technical understanding to engage … they can make the most informed comments that have the most likelihood of influencing the process, and they can also file the lawsuits that can challenge the process."

When the overwhelming majority of interviewees perceive governance as unfair, it's time for a change. Acting in ways that bolster EJ ideals is essential to ensuring a just transition. As aforementioned, the just transition is defined as "ensuring that no one is left behind or pushed behind in the transition to low-carbon and environmentally sustainable economies and societies" (Committee for Development Policy, 2023, p. 1), and EJ is "the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people, regardless of race, culture, national origin, or income, in the development, adoption, implementation, and enforcement of environmental laws, regulations, and policies" (Delta Stewardship Council, n.d.). Further, vulnerability is defined by Delta Adapts as "the intersection of exposure to climate hazards, sensitivity to those hazards, and adaptive capacity, or the ability to recover from and adapt to climate hazards. Delta Adapts identifies the communities with the highest social vulnerability to climate hazards, meaning the communities with high sensitivity and low adaptive capacity to flooding, extreme heat, and wildfire" (Delta Stewardship Council, 2021, p. xi).

Historically, the phrase, "first in time, first in right" was commonly used to describe appropriative water rights, meaning that the first people to use a water resource claimed the rights to it. Appropriative water rights conflict with riparian water rights, which grant rights to landowners (Water Education Foundation, n.d.). While Native Tribes were the original stewards of the Delta, they have been forcibly removed from the land and water that is so deeply connected to their belief system (Delta Stewardship Council, 2025). Tribes were also excluded from land ownership; overall, they were effectively barred from legal claim to resource access (Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians et al., 2022). These injustices only mark the beginning of the tribulations Native Tribes and Indigenous communities were forced to endure. Tribal and Indigenous communities are inherently EJ communities.

Other vulnerable communities in the Delta include those with an intersection of socioeconomic factors that hinder their ability to adapt to hazardous environmental exposures. According to Delta Adapts, vulnerability classifications in the Delta range from moderate, to high, to highest vulnerability (Delta Stewardship Council, 2020). It is important to note: all in-Delta communities are vulnerable, to some degree. This, in turn, classifies all in-Delta residents as an EJ community member.

Inclusion of these historically underrepresented or intentionally excluded voices is decision making (equitable representation) is a core tenet of just transitions. Understanding how different communities are affected by changes and adaptation strategies helps ensure the path forward is equitable and just.

EJ intends to address undue burdens: disproportionate negative impacts incurred by different groups of people. These negative impacts can be disproportionately felt by geography, by race and ethnicity, by income level, or other socioeconomic factors. Understanding where and how negative impacts may manifest can inform decision-makers to intervene or choose alternative strategies to avoid these burdens coming to fruition.

regions.text: Metric: Salinity Impacts to in-Delta Drinking Water
Location of Measurement

Point locations for this criterion utilized the in-Delta drinking water system locations identified by the Safe and Affordable Funding for Equity and Resilience (SAFER) program (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2026), as a representation of where in-Delta communities are located. The SAFER program, derived from the Safe and Affordable Drinking Water (SADW) Fund, is a collection of resources established with the goal of securing clean, affordable water across California (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2026). Figure `1 shows the funds that inform and support SAFER, and the resources SAFER provides Californians.
Figure 1. SAFER program funding sources and services. Image obtained from California State Water Resources Control Board (2026).
The SAFER Dashboard is one tool born out of the program to identify failing and at-risk water systems across the state (California Water Boards, 2024). According to California Water Boards (2024):

The Dashboard displays risk drivers for public water systems. The Dashboard includes source data from the State Water Board, the Department of Water Resources, and the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment. The Dashboard is used by internal staff and members of the public to identify and explore Failing and At-Risk public water systems and how they perform in the following risk categories: water quality, accessibility, affordability, and TMF (technical, managerial, and financial) capacity. The Dashboard displays summary statistics of the number of Failing and At-risk public water systems in different risk categories and shows users the locations of these systems.

The systems included in the dashboard are public water systems (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2025). This includes municipal systems that undergo treatment, as well as wells and surface water systems that do not (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2025).

Since the SAFER locations are inland, points for the Just Transitions in the Delta project were moved from the land into the closest channel/body of water, to capture hydrodynamic modeling data output variations between the scenarios. In total, 49 in-Delta point locations were selected. Figure 1 shows the distribution of point locations selected.
Figure 1. Points for analysis, derived from SAFER drinking water system locations.
Metric: Flood Risk
Location of Measurement

While the Salinity Impacts to in-Delta Drinking Water metric observed outcomes at specific points within the Delta, the Flood Risk metric observed the Delta as a whole. This metric assesses in-Delta inundation risk overall.
Metric: Water Age and Temperature
Location of Measurement

This metric assesses in-Delta water age and temperature by five broad Delta regions that are likely to experience HABs when the right combination of factors align. While there are several indicators that promote HABs, this metric focuses on water age and temperature combinations. Temporally, the months flagged for when the likelihood of HABs increases are May through October. The five regions assessed in this metric include:
Suisun Marsh and surrounding wetlands
Franks Tract
South Delta
Lindsey-Cache Slough
McCormack-Williamson Tract

components.text: What are the components of this criterion?

Upon distilling the feedback from EJ community members and advocates, the Just Transitions in the Delta team found metrics they had the capabilities to assess, metrics that other subteams within the Just Transitions in the Delta project were already assessing, and some priorities that, while important, were out of the scope of the Just Transitions in the Delta project. Appendix A contains detailed documentation of the distilled feedback, along with if and how (generally) metrics were being incorporated. The final metrics are listed below.
Three final metrics will be assessed under the EJ & Vulnerable Communities criterion:

Salinity Impacts to in-Delta Drinking Water: Assessment of salinity changes on in-Delta drinking water systems' ability to meet safe drinking water standards, with special attention to impact to communities of variable vulnerability (classified in accordance with the Delta Vulnerability Index).
Flood Risk Attenuation: Identification of inundation likelihood across the Delta.

Water Age and Temperature: Amount of time water stays in the same location throughout the system in combination with water temperature; used as a proxy for conditions favorable for harmful algal bloom (HABs) formation.
Metric: Salinity Impacts to in-Delta Drinking Water

construction.text: In order to effectively facilitate just transitions through promotion of EJ concerns and considerations, hearing real feedback to align with core EJ values was imperative. While there is general consensus in the literature about what burdens EJ communities face, academic literature does not substitute for boots-on-the-ground, real, meaningful interaction with the community members and advocates this project intends to serve. As such, the Just Transitions in the Delta team intentionally sought out perspectives from EJ communities as often as possible. In order to create the EJ criterion most consistently with the real priorities of our specific EJ community members and advocates, the Just Transitions in the Delta team engaged in the following ways:
Intentional interview invitations to members and advocates of EJ communities
Spotlighting of EJ viewpoints at Public Workshop 1 (June, 2024)
Distillation of values and priorities from EJ Workshop feedback to develop initial EJ criterion
Review and Iteration of EJ criterion at Public Workshop 2 (June, 2025)
Periodic Advisory Committee check-in and review

Commitment to this criterion began at the conception of the Just Transitions in the Delta project, with intentional interview invitations to members and advocates of environmental justice and Tribal communities, in order to prioritize less-often heard voices. Of the 49 semi-structured interviews completed, about 20% of the respondents were part of these underrepresented groups. In these interviews, participants were asked questions about their values, drivers of change of salinity, salinity management strategies to explore, and Delta decision-making and governance. The responses to these questions informed the preliminary scenarios in this project, which were refined through multiple rounds of iteration in subsequent public workshops and forums.

With the intention of increasing participation of less-often heard voices, the Just Transitions in the Delta team held an EJ-focused workshop in December of 2024. At this workshop, participants discussed issues facing EJ and vulnerable communities, and priorities were relayed to the Just Transitions in the Delta Team.

In order to ensure overall alignment with EJ communities' values, we utilized distilled feedback from the Environmental Justice Workshop (December, 2024), Public Workshop #2 (June, 2025), and ongoing collaboration with EJ community members and advocates to highlight the values and priorities of EJ communities. Overall categories of values communicated were water quality and quantity, community and recreation, flood risk, ecological restoration and recovery, ecocultural restoration and Indigenous sovereignty, and sustainable economy and economic transitions. Participants communicated specific components of each of these categories.
